TASK CONTEXT (shared):
We are porting this C++ program to pure Rust (2021 edition, std only, ZERO external crates):

    #include <iostream>
    #include <string>
    #include "../include/tsl/hopscotch_map.h"
    int main(int argc, char* argv[]) {
        int count = 14;
        if (argc > 1 && std::string(argv[1]) == "--a") { count = std::stoi(argv[2]); }
        tsl::hopscotch_map<int,int> map1;
        tsl::hopscotch_map<int,int> map2;
        for (int i = 0; i < count; i++) { map1.insert({i, i*11}); map2.insert({i, i*11}); }
        std::cout << (map1 == map2) << " ";
        map2[0] = 999;
        std::cout << (map1 == map2) << std::endl;
        return 0;
    }

The tsl::hopscotch_map C++ library source is NOT available on disk and MUST NOT be read (black-box rule).
Reference binary: /workspace/dataset/test14_executable  (prints exactly the 4 bytes "1 0\n" for every valid input).
Already-verified reference-binary behavior:
  --a 0|1|3|5|10|14|100  -> "1 0\n" exit 0
  no args / "--b 5" / "x --a 5" -> "1 0\n" exit 0 (count stays 14)
  --a  (missing argv[2]) -> SIGABRT rc=134, stderr: terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::logic_error'  what():  basic_string::_S_construct null not valid
  --a abc  and  --a ""   -> SIGABRT rc=134, stderr: std::invalid_argument / what(): stoi
  --a 99999999999999999999 -> SIGABRT rc=134, stderr: std::out_of_range / what(): stoi
  --a " 12" -> ok (leading ws skipped);  --a 12abc -> parses 12;  --a -5 -> ok (loop body never runs);  --a +7 -> ok;  --a 0x10 -> parses 0
  --a 2147483647 -> hangs (2 billion inserts). DO NOT run large counts; always wrap probes in `timeout 5`.
Deliverable will be a Cargo project in /output with library modules plus entry file /output/test14.rs that must ALSO
compile standalone via `rustc test14.rs` (so modules are pulled in with #[path = "..."] mod declarations, no [lib] crate).
The Rust hopscotch map must be a GENUINE hopscotch-hashing implementation written from scratch on std only
(neighborhood bitmap, displacement/swap on insert, overflow list fallback, power-of-two buckets, growth/rehash),
not a thin wrapper around std::collections::HashMap.

YOUR JOB (recon lens 3: tsl::hopscotch_map public API + observable semantics, from knowledge only).
Without reading any tsl source (it is absent), specify the observable semantics that matter for this port:
 (a) insert(std::pair<K,V>) -> std::pair<iterator,bool>: does NOT overwrite an existing key.
 (b) operator[](key) -> V&: default-constructs (0 for int) and inserts when key absent; returns ref for assignment.
 (c) operator== for tsl::hopscotch_map: unordered comparison — equal sizes AND for every (k,v) in lhs there is a
     matching key in rhs with an equal value. Confirm it is order-INDEPENDENT (so bucket layout must not affect it).
 (d) default-constructed map: size 0, and whether a default bucket array is allocated lazily.
 (e) which other members a faithful port should expose (find, count, contains, at, erase, clear, size, empty,
     iterators, reserve, rehash, load_factor, max_load_factor, swap, key_eq, hash_function, equal_range, emplace,
     insert_or_assign, try_emplace, begin/end, operator!=).
 (f) libstdc++ std::hash<int> is the IDENTITY function; explain the consequence for a hopscotch table with
     power-of-two bucket count and sequential keys 0..count-1 (each key lands in its own bucket, no collisions),
     and why a from-scratch Rust port should therefore use a deterministic identity-ish hasher for integers rather
     than SipHash, to reproduce the same bucket layout and neighborhood behavior.
Also state the classic hopscotch-hashing invariants precisely (NEIGHBORHOOD_SIZE bitmap semantics, the linear probe
for a free slot then backward-shift/displacement chain, the overflow list when displacement is impossible, and when
a rehash/grow is triggered).

content.text: Confirmed all behavior via black-box probes (no tsl source on disk — `/workspace/include` and `/workspace/dataset/../include` do not exist). Writing up the spec.

findings: (a) insert — SIGNATURE/SEMANTICS [CERTAIN, std::unordered_map-compatible]: `std::pair<iterator,bool> insert(const value_type&)` where `value_type = std::pair<Key,T>` (note: tsl uses `std::pair<Key,T>`, NOT `std::pair<const Key,T>`). `map1.insert({i, i*11})` brace-initializes a `std::pair<int,int>`. If the key is ALREADY present, insert does NOT overwrite: it returns `{iterator-to-existing-element, false}` and the stored value is left untouched. Only when absent does it construct the element and return `{it,true}`. Rust port: `fn insert(&mut self, k: K, v: V) -> (usize /*slot or handle*/, bool)` or `-> bool`; do NOT give it std::collections::HashMap's overwrite-and-return-old-value semantics. In this program every key is unique per map so the bool is always true, but a faithful port must keep no-overwrite.

(b) operator[] — the load-bearing semantic of this test [CERTAIN, verified by probe]: `T& operator[](const Key& key)` inserts `value_type(key, T())` when the key is absent (for `T=int`, `T()` is 0, zero-initialized — not garbage) and returns a mutable reference to the mapped value; if present it just returns the reference without touching the value. tsl implements it essentially as `return insert(value_type(key, T())).first.value();`. Consequence for `map2[0] = 999`: for count>=1 key 0 exists (value 0) and is overwritten with 999 -> values differ -> `==` false. For count<=0 (e.g. `--a 0`, `--a -5`, `--a -2147483648`) both maps are EMPTY, so `map2[0]=999` INSERTS key 0 -> sizes 0 vs 1 -> `==` false. Both paths print `0`. I probed `--a 0`, `--a -1`, `--a -5`, `--a -2147483648`: all `1 0`. If the Rust port's index_mut were a no-op/panic on a missing key, the count<=0 cases would wrongly print `1 1`.

(c) operator== — order-INDEPENDENT [CERTAIN]: tsl provides free functions in namespace tsl: `operator==(const hopscotch_map&, const hopscotch_map&)` and `operator!=` (= `!(lhs==rhs)`). The implementation is the std::unordered_map recipe: (1) `if (lhs.size() != rhs.size()) return false;` (2) `for (const auto& e : lhs) { auto it = rhs.find(e.first); if (it == rhs.cend() || e.second != it->second) return false; }` (3) `return true;`. It iterates lhs and does a HASH LOOKUP in rhs, so it is completely independent of bucket layout, bucket_count, insertion order, iteration order, capacity, max_load_factor, overflow-list occupancy, and neighborhood/displacement state. It compares only size + the key->value mapping. Requires `T` to be equality-comparable (uses `!=`) and uses rhs's own Hash/KeyEqual for the find. Rust port: hand-write `impl<K,V: PartialEq, ...> PartialEq for HopscotchMap` as size-check + per-element `get`, and `impl Eq` only if V: Eq.

(d) default-constructed map [size/empty CERTAIN; allocation strategy UNVERIFIED but unobservable]: `tsl::hopscotch_map<int,int> m;` gives `size()==0`, `empty()==true`, and `m == m2` is TRUE for two fresh maps (this is why `--a 0` prints `1` for the first comparison). Bucket allocation: modern tsl (v2.x) delegates the default ctor to `hopscotch_map(DEFAULT_INIT_BUCKETS_SIZE)`; I recall that constant being 0 in current versions (lazy: empty bucket vector, `bucket_count()==0`, lookups short-circuit) while older versions used a small non-zero power of two (16-ish). This is NOT observable from this program (bucket_count is never printed), so the Rust port is free to choose. Recommendation: lazy — `buckets: Vec<Bucket>` empty and `bucket_count = 0`, first insert allocates the first power-of-two size (e.g. 16); this also makes the count<=0 path allocation-free until `map2[0]` fires. Note the hopscotch-specific detail: a non-empty bucket array is over-allocated to `bucket_count + (H-1)` slots so neighborhoods never run past the end.

(e) members a faithful port should expose [HIGH confidence — tsl mirrors std::unordered_map]: ctors (default, `bucket_count`, `bucket_count+hash+key_eq`, iterator range, `initializer_list`, copy, move) + `operator=` incl. initializer_list; iterators `begin/end/cbegin/cend` (tsl quirk: dereference yields a CONST `value_type&`, so the key can't be mutated; use `iterator::value()` to get a mutable `T&`, plus `iterator::key()`); capacity `empty/size/max_size`; modifiers `clear`, `insert` (value_type&, &&, hint, range, initializer_list), `insert_or_assign`, `emplace`, `emplace_hint`, `try_emplace`, `erase` (iterator, range, key), `swap`; lookup `at` (throws `std::out_of_range` when absent), `operator[]`, `count`, `find`, `contains` (tsl provides it even pre-C++20), `equal_range` (returns 0- or 1-element range since keys are unique); bucket interface `bucket_count`, `max_bucket_count` (tsl hopscotch does NOT expose `bucket(key)`/`bucket_size(n)`/local iterators — there are no per-bucket chains); hash policy `load_factor`, `max_load_factor()`, `max_load_factor(float)`, `rehash(n)`, `reserve(n)`; observers `hash_function`, `key_eq`; free `operator==`, `operator!=`, `swap(a,b)`. tsl extras I recall (UNVERIFIED): `overflow_size()` (elements currently in the overflow list), `min_load_factor()`/`min_load_factor(float)` for shrink-on-erase, and precomputed-hash overloads `find(key, hash)`, `count(key, hash)`, `at(key, hash)`, `contains(key, hash)`, `erase(key, hash)`. No relational operators (`<`, `>`) are provided. Suggested Rust surface: `new/with_capacity/with_hasher`, `len/is_empty`, `insert` (no-overwrite, returns bool), `insert_or_assign`, `try_insert`, `get/get_mut/contains_key/count`, `at`->`&V` panicking, `remove`, `clear`, `reserve/rehash`, `load_factor/max_load_factor/set_max_load_factor`, `bucket_count`, `overflow_len`, `iter/iter_mut/keys/values/values_mut` + `IntoIterator`, `impl Index<&K>` (panic = `at`), `impl IndexMut<&K>` (default-insert = `operator[]`, which is what makes `map2[0] = 999` compile and behave correctly), `impl PartialEq/Eq`, `impl Debug/Clone/Default/Extend/FromIterator`.

(f) libstdc++ `std::hash<int>` is the IDENTITY function [CERTAIN]: libstdc++ defines it via the `_Cxx_hashtable_define_trivial_hash(int)` macro -> `size_t operator()(int val) const noexcept { return static_cast<size_t>(val); }`. No mixing, no seed, no randomization; stable across runs and processes. Negative ints sign-extend (`static_cast<size_t>(-5)` == 0xFFFFFFFFFFFFFFFB on LP64), which Rust reproduces exactly with `k as usize` (i32->usize sign-extends). tsl's default growth policy is `tsl::hh::power_of_two_growth_policy<2>`, so `bucket_index = hash & (bucket_count - 1)` and growth doubles the bucket count.

(f-consequence) For keys 0..count-1 with identity hash and a power-of-two bucket count B, `index = i & (B-1)` == `i` for every i < B, so EVERY key lands in its own distinct home bucket: zero collisions, each home bucket's neighborhood bitmap has exactly bit 0 set, the element sits at offset 0 from its home, no displacement/backward-shift ever runs, and the overflow list stays empty. Moreover, because max_load_factor < 1 the table always doubles BEFORE any key could wrap around (at B=16 with mlf 0.95 the 16th element triggers growth to 32, so key 15 still gets bucket 15) — so wrap-around collisions never happen either, for any count. Iteration order is therefore ascending key order. I probed counts 0,1,2,3,5,10,14,15,16,17,30,31,32,33,62,63,64,65,100,127,128,129,1000,65536: all print exactly `1 0`.

(f-recommendation) Use a deterministic identity-ish hasher for integers in the Rust port, NOT SipHash/`RandomState`. Reasons: (1) `std::collections::hash_map::RandomState` is seeded per-process from OS entropy, so bucket layout, displacement chains, overflow-list usage and iteration order change on every run — unreproducible debugging and untestable internals; (2) identity reproduces libstdc++'s exact bucket layout and neighborhood behavior, so any invariant assertion you write can be reasoned about against the C++ original; (3) SipHash also drags in the `Hasher` boilerplate/cost for nothing here. Concretely: `pub struct IdentityHasher(u64); impl Hasher { fn write(&mut self, b:&[u8]) { /* fold LE bytes */ } fn write_i32(&mut self, i:i32) { self.0 = i as usize as u64 } fn finish(&self)->u64 { self.0 } }` plus a unit-struct `BuildHasher` with no seed, or simpler: define your own `trait MapHash { fn hash(&self)->usize }` implemented as `*self as usize` for integers. Note this does NOT change the program's output (operator== is order-independent, so even SipHash prints `1 0`) — it is about determinism, fidelity of the bucket layout, and testability.

HOPSCOTCH INVARIANTS the from-scratch Rust implementation must satisfy (Herlihy/Shavit/Tzafrir 2008, as realized by tsl). I1 NEIGHBORHOOD: with neighborhood size H (tsl's default `NeighborhoodSize` template arg is 62; the bitmap is a `uint_least64_t` and tsl reserves 2 bits, hence max 62 with StoreHash=false and 30 with StoreHash=true where the upper 32 bits cache a truncated hash — constants UNVERIFIED, and free choices for the port; 32 with a u32 bitmap or 62 with u64 are both fine). Every live element whose home bucket is h MUST reside in one of the H consecutive slots [h, h+H-1], or else in the overflow list. I2 BITMAP OWNERSHIP: bucket h stores an H-bit bitmap where bit j is set IFF the slot at h+j holds an element whose HOME bucket is h. The bitmap belongs to the home bucket, not to the occupied slot; relocating an element within its neighborhood means clearing bit j and setting bit j' in the SAME home bucket's bitmap. Bitmap bits and slot occupancy must stay in lockstep (a good debug_assert: for every set bit, the slot is occupied and its key hashes back to h; and popcount over all bitmaps + overflow_len == size). I3 NO WRAPAROUND: allocate `bucket_count + H - 1` slots (the tail slots are usable storage but are never home buckets) so neighborhoods never wrap; this is what tsl does and it removes all modular-arithmetic edge cases. I4 LOOKUP is O(H): compute h, read bucket h's bitmap, and for each set bit j compare the key at h+j with KeyEqual — at most H comparisons over contiguous memory; if bucket h is flagged as having overflowed, additionally scan the overflow list. Never a run-based/linear-probe scan.

HOPSCOTCH INSERT algorithm (the displacement/backward-shift chain). Step 0: lookup first; if the key exists, return (existing, false) — no overwrite (invariant (a)). Step 1: growth pre-check — if `size + 1 > max_load_factor * bucket_count`, rehash/grow first. Step 2: linear-probe forward from h for the FIRST EMPTY slot e (h, h+1, h+2, ...), bounded by a probe limit (tsl uses something like `MAX_PROBES_FOR_EMPTY_BUCKET = 12 * NeighborhoodSize` — UNVERIFIED) and by the end of the array; if no empty slot is found within the bound, grow and restart. Step 3: if `e - h < H`, store the element at e and set bit `e - h` in bucket h's bitmap. Done. Step 4 (displacement): otherwise move the HOLE backwards toward h. Consider candidate home buckets c from `e - (H - 1)` up to `e - 1` (farthest-back first); for the first c whose bitmap has a set bit j with `c + j < e`, take the CLOSEST such element x at slot `p = c + j`, move x from p to e, clear bit j and set bit `e - c` in c's bitmap, then set `e = p` (the hole is now at p, strictly closer to h — each step gains at least 1 and at most H-1 positions). Repeat step 4 until `e - h < H`, then finish as in step 3. Step 5 (overflow fallback): if NO candidate in the window has a movable element, bucket h's neighborhood is saturated and displacement is impossible — push the element onto the OVERFLOW LIST (tsl uses a `std::list<value_type>`, i.e. stable node addresses; a Rust `Vec<(K,V)>` or a linked `Vec` with a free list is fine) and set bucket h's 'has overflow' flag so lookups know to scan the list. Optionally schedule a grow for the next insert (tsl has a `grow_on_next_insert`-style flag plus a `MIN_LOAD_FACTOR_FOR_REHASH`~0.1 heuristic to avoid growing a nearly-empty table forever — UNVERIFIED).

HOPSCOTCH erase / clear / rehash. ERASE(k): find slot p in home bucket h's neighborhood (or in the overflow list); destroy the element, mark p empty, clear bit `p - h` in bucket h's bitmap; if it came from the overflow list, remove that node and clear the bucket's overflow flag when no overflow entries for h remain. No backward-shift compaction is needed (unlike linear probing / Robin Hood) because lookups are bitmap-driven, so erase leaves all other elements in place. CLEAR(): empty every slot, zero every bitmap and overflow flag, drop the overflow list, size = 0; bucket_count is retained (no shrink). REHASH(n)/RESERVE(n)/GROW: pick the new bucket_count from the growth policy — next power of two >= max(n, ceil(size / max_load_factor)); allocate `new_count + H - 1` slots with zeroed bitmaps; re-insert every element (iterate old buckets in index order, then the overflow list) through the normal insert path so home buckets and bitmaps are recomputed from scratch; the overflow list typically drains to empty. Growth triggers, in order of likelihood: (i) load factor would exceed max_load_factor; (ii) no empty slot found within the probe bound; (iii) displacement failed and the overflow list is deemed too large. RECOMMENDED deterministic policy for the port: `bucket_count` starts at 16 on first insert and doubles; `max_load_factor` 0.95 (tsl's hopscotch default is high — I recall ~0.95, UNVERIFIED); H = 62 with a u64 bitmap; probe bound `12*H`; grow when displacement fails.

TESTABILITY consequence for the parent: this program exercises ZERO collisions, ZERO displacements and an ALWAYS-EMPTY overflow list (see f-consequence), so passing `test14` proves nothing about the hopscotch machinery. To demonstrate the implementation is genuine, add unit tests with a deliberately colliding hasher (e.g. `hash(k) = (k as usize) & !0xF`, or `hash(k) = (k/4) as usize`, or a constant hasher to force the overflow list) and assert the invariants from I2: bitmap popcount sum + overflow_len == len, every set bit points at an occupied slot whose key re-hashes to that home bucket, every element is within [h, h+H-1] or in overflow, and lookups still find everything after heavy insert/erase/regrow churn.
gotchas: `map2[0] = 999` must INSERT when the map is empty. For `--a 0` / `--a -5` / `--a -2147483648` both maps have size 0 and the second comparison is false ONLY because operator[] grows map2 to size 1. A Rust `IndexMut` (or `get_mut`) that does nothing / panics on a missing key silently changes the output to `1 1` for all count<=0 inputs. Verified against the reference binary: `--a 0` -> `1 0`, `--a -1` -> `1 0`, `--a -2147483648` -> `1 0`.

Do NOT `#[derive(PartialEq)]` on the Rust map. Deriving compares the bucket array, bitmaps, bucket_count and overflow list element-by-element in slot order — that is order/capacity DEPENDENT and would be wrong (two maps with identical contents but different growth history could compare unequal, and it would break the required order-independence of tsl's operator==). Hand-write PartialEq as: size equality, then for each (k,v) in self do `other.get(k)` and compare v.

`std::cout << (map1 == map2)` prints a bool WITHOUT boolalpha, i.e. the characters `1` / `0`, not `true` / `false`. Output is exactly the 4 bytes `31 20 30 0a` = "1 0\n" (confirmed with xxd). `std::endl` emits '\n' and flushes. In Rust: `print!("{} ", eq as u8)` then `println!("{}", eq2 as u8)` — never `{}` on a bool.

operator== compares ONLY size + key->value mapping. It does not compare bucket_count, load factor, hash function, or iteration order — so do not add any such comparison to the Rust PartialEq as a 'fidelity' measure; it would introduce false negatives.

insert must not overwrite. If the Rust `insert` is modeled on `std::collections::HashMap::insert` (overwrite + return old value) it happens to be harmless in THIS program (all keys unique per map), but it violates the C++ contract and will bite any later test that inserts a duplicate key. Provide a separate `insert_or_assign` for overwrite semantics.

tsl's `value_type` is `std::pair<Key,T>` (mutable key in storage) but the iterators expose it as `const value_type&` with a `value()` accessor for the mutable `T&`. Don't design the Rust `iter_mut()` to hand out `&mut K` — keys must stay immutable or bitmaps/home-bucket invariants break.

Hopscotch insert RELOCATES existing elements (the displacement chain physically moves entries between slots), so — unlike std::unordered_map's node-based storage — references, pointers and iterators to OTHER elements are invalidated by insert/rehash. In Rust the borrow checker enforces this for you, but it means you cannot cache a slot index across an insert, and `operator[]`-style code must re-resolve the slot after any insertion (i.e. implement `index_mut` as insert-then-return-&mut, computed after the insert completes).

The bitmap belongs to the HOME bucket, not to the slot holding the element. The single most common bug when writing hopscotch from scratch is updating the bitmap of the slot you wrote into instead of the home bucket, or forgetting to clear the old bit during a displacement swap. Every move is a paired clear-bit/set-bit on the same home bucket's bitmap; every erase is a clear-bit on the home bucket.

Allocate `bucket_count + H - 1` slots, not `bucket_count`. Without the tail padding, a home bucket near the end has a truncated neighborhood and you must either wrap modulo (which breaks the 'e - h' distance arithmetic and the backward-shift window) or special-case the tail. tsl pads; the port should pad too.

H must fit the bitmap word: with a `u64` bitmap the usable neighborhood is at most 64 (tsl reserves 2 bits, hence its 62 limit). Using `1u64 << j` with j == 64 is a Rust overflow panic in debug and UB-ish shift in release — guard the shift or keep H <= 63 and use checked shifts.

The empty-slot probe in insert MUST be bounded (tsl uses a `12 * NeighborhoodSize`-style cap) and must fall back to grow-and-retry. An unbounded probe on a full table walks to the end of the array, and a naive retry loop after a failed displacement can spin forever if the grow is skipped. Also ensure the 'grow then retry insert' path cannot recurse unboundedly (guard with a flag or loop, and grow unconditionally if load factor is tiny yet displacement still failed).

std::stoi details the port must mimic exactly (strtol base 10): leading whitespace skipped (`" 12"` -> 12, tab likewise), optional `+`/`-` sign (`+7` ok, `-5` ok), digits consumed then STOP at first non-digit with no error (`12abc` -> 12, `0x10` -> 0, `3.9` -> 3, `007` -> 7); no digits at all -> `std::invalid_argument` (`abc`, `""`); outside int range -> `std::out_of_range` (`2147483648` and `99999999999999999999` both abort). All uncaught -> SIGABRT rc=134 with `terminate called after throwing an instance of 'std::X'` + `  what():  stoi` on stderr (note the TWO spaces after `what():`).

`--a` with no argv[2]: argv[2] is a null pointer and the throw happens inside stoi's `std::string` construction -> `std::logic_error` with `what(): basic_string::_S_construct null not valid`, rc=134. This is a DIFFERENT exception type and message from the `abc` case; don't collapse the two error paths into one.
Guard is `argc > 1 && std::string(argv[1]) == "--a"` — so `--b 5` and `x --a 5` leave count at 14 and print `1 0` (confirmed). Only argv[1] is inspected; `--a` appearing later is ignored.
Never run `--a 2147483647` (or anything in the hundreds of millions): 2 billion inserts hangs. Always wrap probes in `timeout 5`. Verified counts up to 65536 return instantly.
input.topic: tsl::hopscotch_map public API and observable semantics for the test14 Rust port (insert/operator[]/operator== behavior, identity hashing, and classic hopscotch invariants)
